title: How UK resolution planning allocates losses while keeping deposits accessible
summary: Ruth Smith, the Bank of England's Executive Director for Resolution, argues that preserving a failing bank's critical functions requires more than a stock of loss-absorbing debt. The authorities must be able to recapitalise or transfer the business, supply liquidity where appropriate and keep customers able to make payments, sometimes within days. Those objectives can favour a different intervention at the point of failure from the strategy chosen in advance. For holders of UK financial credit, the resulting questions are specific to each institution. Where does a claim rank? How would the bank be resolved? Would a transfer be operationally feasible under the speed of the run? The article sets out the rules and the limits of what pre-crisis planning can predict (“Introduction” and “Resolution strategies”).

The starting point is the creditor hierarchy and the public interest in continuity. For the largest and most complex firms, the Bank expects to convert eligible liabilities into equity through bail-in, restoring capital while the underlying business is restructured, potentially over several years. The revised policy effective 1 January generally points to this strategy above £40 billion of total assets. The minimum requirement for own funds and eligible liabilities, MREL, makes the firm's shareholders and investors supply resources in advance. Eligibility depends on maturity, form and where the resources sit in the group. A minimum one-year maturity helps keep them available. This capacity to allocate losses is distinct from the cash needed to meet withdrawals during a resolution.

A transfer can put some or all of the business into the hands of another bank. If a purchaser is unavailable the Bank can temporarily hold the business in a bridge bank before selling it. In the £25 billion to £40 billion asset range the choice between transfer and bail-in is individual. Simplicity, attractiveness to bidders and the ability to deliver information promptly all matter. Below that range, insolvency may be suitable where the failure would create little wider disruption and the firm provides limited critical services. Protected depositors receive priority through an FSCS payout or account transfer, followed by an ordinary winding-up of the rest. The amounts are indicative thresholds applied alongside a public-interest test. A particular recovery cannot be read from balance-sheet size alone.

Two protections act at different levels. Losses follow the statutory ranking. Separately, a creditor that receives less in resolution than it would have in insolvency can be entitled to compensation. The Treasury would pay any such compensation and recover it from the industry. This benchmark protects the counterfactual insolvency value rather than promising the creditor repayment at par. Temporary public funding remains possible as a last resort in severe circumstances. The January policy removes additional MREL requirements for firms on a transfer strategy. The 2025 recapitalisation legislation allows industry-funded support when a small failure would otherwise require a disorderly insolvency. Smith presents the former as self-insurance by large firms and the latter as a collective safety net (“The introduction of MREL”).

Silicon Valley Bank UK showed why formal deposit protection cannot by itself secure continuity. Eligible depositors had protection up to £120,000 at the time of publication. A customer making frequent payments could still be severely disrupted by a period without account access. In the 2023 episode the Bank prepared both insolvency and transfer while outflows accelerated. An ability to identify records, share them with bidders and switch plans in time therefore has economic value. Under the Resolvability Assessment Framework firms are responsible for demonstrating financial resources, operational continuity and effective communication. Major banks publish assessments. Smith argues that a credible resolution alternative can also strengthen incentives for shareholders and creditors to find private solutions before authorities have to act (“The importance of flexibility in resolution strategies”).

Credit Suisse illustrates the cross-border complication. The Swiss authorities ultimately selected a going-concern sale to UBS. The UK authorities had prepared to give legal effect to a home-country resolution in the UK had that been necessary. That preparation is evidence of operational readiness, rather than an observed test of a completed cross-border bail-in. Crisis management groups, joint exercises and rehearsed communications become material when decisions in one country must quickly take legal and operational effect in another. The article closes with emerging challenges, including faster digital withdrawals and the growth of private credit. For central counterparties, there are overlapping safeguards and coordination needs, but the UK has distinct powers such as cash calls and contract tear-up. The bank-credit loss waterfall alone does not explain the risks to clearing participants.

questions.question: Could this bank actually be transferred over a stressed weekend?
questions.detail: The indicative asset ranges leave room for a firm-specific decision, and the SVB UK case shows how quickly authorities may have to switch strategies. Review the bank's public resolvability disclosures, the complexity of its legal entities and any evidence about data availability and potential acquirers. A realistic transfer option changes the set of possible outcomes for creditors even where the public interest in keeping deposits accessible is strong.

questions.question: How much usable liquidity would remain after the first wave of withdrawals?
questions.detail: The article identifies both loss-absorbing resources and liquidity as conditions for execution. It gives no institution-level calculation of immediately usable collateral or the pace of uninsured outflows. Compare the firm's funding and liquidity disclosures with its collateral arrangements, depositor concentration and operational testing. Maturity and encumbrance matter for how much time the authorities would have to organise an orderly resolution.

questions.question: Which legal entity and jurisdiction would determine the claim's recovery?
questions.detail: Smith describes creditor ranking, the insolvency counterfactual and the coordination required of home and host authorities. She does not estimate recoveries for a particular debt issue. Use issuer prospectuses, legal entity accounts, MREL disclosures and public resolution plans to locate the claim and the resources that rank ahead of it. In a cross-border group, check where recognition of an overseas action would be needed.
